description.sr_latin: Fraze za jutarnje rutine, kućne poslove, večernje opuštanje i zajednički život.
description.en: Phrases for morning routines, household chores, evening chill time, and living together.

phrases.context: Your partner has slept through the alarm and you shake them awake with a sharp nudge.
phrases.notes: 'Ustaj' = get up (imperative of 'ustati'). Direct and casual — the everyday wake-up bark.

phrases.context: Someone is trying to drag you out of bed and you bargain for a little more sleep.
phrases.notes: 'Još' = more/still. 'Minuta' is genitive plural after 'pet' — numbers above four take the genitive.

phrases.context: You're up first and you offer to put the morning coffee on for your partner.
phrases.notes: 'Kafu' is the accusative object of 'hoćeš'. 'Kafa' comes from Turkish; Croatians say 'kava', Bosnians 'kahva'.

phrases.context: You're still buried in the blanket and you sweetly ask your partner to bring you coffee.
phrases.notes: 'Napravi' = make (imperative of 'napraviti'). 'Mi' is the dative 'for me'; 'molim te' keeps it soft.

phrases.en: Who's going to the bathroom first?
phrases.context: You both need to get ready and there's one bathroom, so you sort out the order.
phrases.notes: 'U kupatilo' takes the accusative for motion 'into'. Bosnians often say 'kupaonica' instead of 'kupatilo'.

phrases.context: Your partner is dawdling and you're about to miss the bus, so you push them to speed up.
phrases.notes: 'Požuri' = hurry (imperative). 'Kasnim' = I'm late, present tense of 'kasniti' used for right now.

phrases.context: You're both getting dressed and you ask your partner what they're putting on.
phrases.notes: 'Oblačiti' = to put on (clothes). The present tense covers 'are you going to wear' here.

phrases.context: You wander into the kitchen and ask what there is to eat first thing.
phrases.notes: Impersonal 'ima' = 'there is'. 'Doručak' = breakfast; 'ručak' = lunch, 'večera' = dinner.

phrases.context: You shuffle in starving before anything's on the table and groan how ravenous you are.
phrases.notes: 'Gladan' is the masculine form; a woman says 'gladna'. The adjective agrees with the speaker's gender.

phrases.en: I cook, you wash the dishes.
phrases.context: You're splitting kitchen duty with your partner and you call who does what.
phrases.notes: 'Pereš sudove' = you wash the dishes (accusative plural). The 'kuham/kuhati' h-form is Bosnian/Croatian; in Serbia it's 'kuvam/kuvati'.

phrases.context: A pile of plates is sitting in the sink and you ask whose turn it is tonight.
phrases.notes: 'Prati sudove' = to wash the dishes; 'pere' is the 3sg present. 'Sudove' is accusative plural of 'sud'.

phrases.context: The floor is covered in crumbs and you tell your partner it's time to clean up.
phrases.notes: 'Treba da' + present = 'we need to'. 'Usisati' = to vacuum, from 'sisati' (to suck).

phrases.context: The bin is overflowing on your way out and you ask your partner to deal with it.
phrases.notes: 'Iznesi' = take out (imperative of 'izneti'). 'Đubre' is a Turkish loanword that originally meant 'manure'.

phrases.sr_latin: Veš neće sam sebe da opere.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Веш неће сам себе да опере.
phrases.context: A full basket has sat untouched for days and you drop a pointed hint to your partner.
phrases.notes: 'Neće' = won't (negative of 'hoće'). 'Sam sebe' = itself; this dry sarcasm is very natural in Serbian. 'Veš' is from German 'Wäsche'.

phraseGroups.theme: Asking Your Partner to Do Something

phrases.sr_latin: Možeš li da odeš do prodavnice?
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Можеш ли да одеш до продавнице?
phrases.en: Can you go to the store?
phrases.context: You realize you're out of something and ask your partner to pop out for it.
phrases.notes: 'Možeš li da...' = 'can you...'. 'Do prodavnice' takes the genitive after 'do' (up to/as far as).

phrases.context: You're wrestling with something around the flat and you ask your partner to lend a hand.
phrases.notes: 'Pomozi' = help (imperative of 'pomoći'). 'Pomoći' takes the dative — you help 'to' someone, 'mi'.

phrases.sr_latin: Može da skuvaš nešto za večeru?
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Може да скуваш нешто за вечеру?
phrases.en: Could you cook something for dinner?
phrases.context: You're swamped and you nudge your partner to take over the cooking tonight.
phrases.notes: 'Može da...' is softer and more colloquial than 'možeš li da...'. 'Skuvati' (Serbian) vs Bosnian/Croatian 'skuhati'.

phrases.context: You've both collapsed on the couch after dinner and you suggest putting a show on.
phrases.notes: 'Ajde da' + 1pl present = 'let's...', one of the most useful casual frames. 'Ajde' is a clipped 'hajde'.

phrases.en: What do you want to watch?
phrases.context: The remote is in your partner's hands and you let them pick tonight's show.
phrases.notes: 'Ćeš da...' uses the future clitic 'ćeš' — literally 'what will you watch', meaning 'what do you feel like watching'.

phrases.sr_latin: Umoran sam, ceo dan sam radio.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Уморан сам, цео дан сам радио.
phrases.en: I'm tired, I worked all day.
phrases.context: You flop onto the couch and explain to your partner why you've got nothing left tonight.
phrases.notes: 'Radio' is the masculine past participle; 'sam radio' = I worked. A woman says 'umorna sam... radila'.

variations.sr_latin: Umorna sam, ceo dan sam radila.
variations.sr_cyrillic: Уморна сам, цео дан сам радила.
variations.en: I'm tired, I worked all day.

phrases.context: Your partner has been hogging the channels and you reach out for the remote.
phrases.notes: 'Daj mi' = give me ('mi' is dative). 'Daljinski' is short for 'daljinski upravljač' (remote control).

phrases.context: It's late and you're both yawning, so you suggest calling it a night.
phrases.notes: 'Ajde da spavamo' = let's go to sleep (literally 'let's sleep'). 'Spavati' = to sleep.

phrases.context: You're heading off to bed and you say the plain bedtime line that works with anyone.
phrases.notes: Frozen accusative wish — 'laku noć' literally '(I wish you) an easy night', like 'dobar dan'.

phrases.context: You're already tucked in and you ask your partner to kill the lights before sleep.
phrases.notes: 'Ugasiti' = to turn off / extinguish; also used for the TV or phone. 'Svetlo' (Serbian) vs Bosnian/Croatian 'svjetlo'.

phrases.context: You're lying awake tossing and turning and tell your partner sleep just won't come.
phrases.notes: 'Ne mogu da...' = 'I can't...', a very common frame: negate 'mogu' and follow with 'da' + present.

phrases.context: You're already late and patting your pockets in a panic by the front door.
phrases.notes: 'Ključevi' is the nominative plural of 'ključ' (key); short masculine nouns add '-ev-' in the plural.

phrases.context: Your partner is heading out last and you remind them to secure the front door.
phrases.notes: 'Zaključaj' = lock (imperative). 'Vrata' is neuter plural — always plural, even for a single door.

phrases.context: Your partner is still out and you text to find out when they'll be back.
phrases.notes: 'Kući' (dative) means 'homeward' for motion. 'Kod kuće' would be 'at home', no motion.

phrases.context: You open the fridge, find the carton empty, and flag that you need to restock.
phrases.notes: 'Ponestati' takes the dative experiencer ('nam' = to us) and a genitive of what ran out ('mleka'). Bosnians say 'mlijeko' / 'mlijeka'.

phrases.context: Your friend asks if you're up for plans and you declare a full day parked at home.
phrases.notes: Double negative is required: 'ne... nigde' = not... nowhere. 'Izlaziti' = to go out.

phrases.context: Your partner asks the plan and you announce the dress code is staying in your PJs.
phrases.notes: 'U pidžami' is locative (state of being in), not motion. 'Pidžama' comes ultimately from Persian via Turkish.

phrases.context: Neither of you feels like cooking, so you float the idea of getting food delivered.
phrases.notes: 'Naručiti' = to order; works for delivery, a restaurant, or online shopping. 'Hoćeš da...' invites the other person in.

phrases.sr_latin: Ma hajde da ležimo ceo dan.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Ма хајде да лежимо цео дан.
phrases.en: Let's just lie around all day.
phrases.context: There's nothing on the calendar and you talk your partner into doing absolutely nothing.
phrases.notes: 'Ležati' = to lie down/around. Opening 'ma' adds a breezy, dismissive 'oh come on' tone.

phrases.context: Your partner walks in the door at the end of the day and you want to hear how it went.
phrases.notes: 'Dan' is masculine, so the past participle is 'bio'. 'Ti' here is the dative 'to you' — literally 'how was the day to you'.

phrases.context: You're catching up over dinner and ask your partner what filled their day.
phrases.notes: Past tense: 'si radio' = you did/were doing. 'Radio' is the masculine participle; to a woman it's 'radila'.

phrases.sr_latin: Baš sam se smorio na poslu.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Баш сам се сморио на послу.
phrases.en: I was so bored at work.
phrases.context: You drop onto the sofa and vent to your partner about a deadly dull day at the office.
phrases.notes: 'Smoriti se' = to get bored/fed up, very colloquial; 'smorio' is masculine, 'smorila' feminine. 'Na poslu' is locative.

variations.sr_latin: Baš sam se smorila na poslu.
variations.sr_cyrillic: Баш сам се сморила на послу.
variations.en: I was so bored at work.
